months.name: January
epigraph: St. Agnes’ Eve—Ah, bitter chill it was!
The owl, for all his feathers, was a-cold;
The hare limp’d trembling through the frozen grass,
And silent was the flock in woolly fold. . .

months.name: February
epigraph: . . . howling Winter fled afar
To hills that prop the polar star;
And loves on deer-borne car to ride
With barren darkness at his side . . .
. . . sullen Winter! hear my prayer,
And gently rule the ruin’d year . . .

months.name: March
epigraph: Old Winter back to the savage hills
Withdraweth his force, decrepid now.

months.name: April
epigraph: . . . proud-pied April, dress’d in all his trim,
Hath put a spirit of youth in everything,
That heavy Saturn laughed and leaped with him.

months.name: May
epigraph: When the hounds of spring are on winter’s traces,
The mother of months in meadow or plain
Fills the shadows and windy places
With lisp of leaves and ripple of rain. . .

months.name: June
epigraph: When shepherds pipe on oaten straws,
And merry larks are ploughmen’s clocks,
When turtles tread, and rooks, and daws,
And maidens bleach their summer smocks.

months.name: July
epigraph: Rosy summer next advancing, . . .
On Calpe’s olive-shaded steep
Or India’s citron-cover’d isles. . . .

months.name: August
epigraph: Now westlin winds and slaught’ring guns
Bring Autumn’s pleasant weather. . . .
Now waving grain, wide o’er the plain,
Delights the weary farmer. . . .

months.name: September
epigraph: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness,
Close bosom-friend of the maturing sun;
Conspiring with him how to load and bless
With fruit the vines that round the thatch-eaves run. . .

months.name: October
epigraph: The skies they were ashen and sober;
The leaves they were crispèd and sere—
The leaves they were withering and sere. . .

months.name: November
epigraph: When biting Boreas, fell and dour,
Sharp shivers thro’ the leafless bow’r;
When Phœbus gies a short-liv’d glow’r,
Far south the lift,
Dim-dark’ning thro’ the flaky show’r,
Or whirling drift.

months.name: December
epigraph: When icicles hang by the wall
And Dick the shepherd blows his nail,
And Tom bears logs into the hall,
And milk comes frozen home in pail. . .

days.title: Franklin’s Advice for the New Year
intro: “Resolution: Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve”—was one of the rules for success framed by America’s first “self-made” man.

days.title: School-Day Poems of John Milton
intro: At the age of sixteen, Milton first appeared before the public eye as a promising young poet. These early verses, written while he was a boy in school, indicate his brilliant future.
notes: First edition of Milton’s collected poems published Jan. 2, 1645.

days.title: Cicero on Friendship
intro: “Fire and water are not of more universal use than friendship”—such is the high value put upon this great human relationship by the most famous orator of Rome.

days.title: A Flounder Fish Story
intro: A fisherman, so the story goes, once caught a flounder that spoke, begging to be released. This was granted, whereupon the fisherman’s wife demanded that it grant her one miracle after another, until even the flounder was disgusted.
notes: Jacob Grimm, elder of the famous Grimm brothers, born Jan. 4, 1785.

days.title: The Soaring Eagle and Contented Stork
intro: Mazzini labored for the freedom of Italy, but was exiled. Byron and Goethe also battled for liberty. Mazzini wrote an essay in which he compared Byron to a soaring eagle and Goethe to a contented stork.
notes: Byron arrived in Greece to fight for Greek freedom, Jan. 5, 1824.

days.title: Warned by Hector’s Ghost
intro: In the dead of night Hector’s ghost appeared to warn Æneas of the impending doom to come upon the walled city of Troy. Æneas lifted his aged father on his back and, taking his son by the hand, sought safety in flight. Off to Latium!
notes: H. Schliemann, discoverer of ancient Troy, born Jan. 6, 1822.

days.title: If He Yawned, She Lost Her Head!
intro: The Sultan had a habit of beheading each dawn his beautiful bride of the night before, until he encountered Scheherazade. Cleverly she saved her life a thousand and one mornings.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: Trying the Patience of Job
intro: God was pleased with the piety of Job, but Satan accredited the piety to Job’s prosperity and happiness. So a trial was made. See how each succeeding affliction visited on Job shook the depths of his nature, and how he survived.
days.printed: Read from The Book of Job

days.title: A Treasure Hunt in Nombre de Dios
intro: With only fifty-two men, Sir Francis Drake conceives the idea of attacking his archenemy, Spain, at her most vulnerable point the treasure at Nombre de Dios.
days.printed: Read from Nichol’s Sir Francis Drake Revived
notes: Drake died at Nombre de Dios, Jan. 9, 1596.

days.title: Where Love Lies Waiting
intro: King Pantheus of Thebes contended against Dionysus, the God, for the adoration of the Theban women. The god was winning by bewitching the women when the king interceded. Euripides tells the story in a masterpiece of Greek drama.

days.title: Hamilton—Father of Wall Street
intro: Hamilton organized the Treasury Department. He penned most of the Federalist papers, which were greatly influential in bringing New York into the Union—the first step toward its eminent position in national and world finance.

days.title: What Is Good Taste?
intro: A Turkish sultan, relates Burke, when shown a picture of the beheaded John the Baptist, praised many things, but pointed out one gruesome defect. Did this observation show the sultan to be an inferior judge of art?

days.title: Rousseau Seeks Sanctuary in England
intro: Rousseau taught that men were not created free and equal. To substantiate his daring beliefs he traced man’s history back to his primitive beginnings. For his teachings, Rousseau was forced to seek refuge in England.
days.printed: Read from Rousseau’s Inquiry on Inequality
notes: Jean Jacques Rousseau arrived in England, Jan. 13, 1766.

days.title: The First Step Toward Independence
intro: The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut is “the first written constitution as a permanent limitation on governmental power, known in history.” It is the work of the Connecticut Yankee.
days.printed: Read: The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut
notes: Fundamental Orders of Connecticut adopted Jan. 14, 1639.

days.title: “The Moving Finger Writes”
intro: Omar Khayyam laughed and enjoyed the good things of life. His “Rubaiyat,” the most popular philosophic poem, is the best of all books to dip into for an alluring thought.
days.printed: Read from The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam
notes: “Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam” first published Jan. 15, 1859.

days.title: The Old Woman and the Wine Jar
intro: An old woman once found a wine jar, but it was empty. She sniffed at the mouth of the jar and said: “What memories cling ’round the instruments of our pleasure.”

days.title: Franklin’s Family Tree
intro: Good middle-class people, Franklin boasts, were his ancestors. Some have attributed his genius to his being the youngest son of the youngest son for five generations. In his famous autobiography, he reveals quaint family history.

days.title: Origin of Yale “Brekekekex-Ko-ax”
intro: “Shall I crack any of those old jokes, master, at which the audience never fails to laugh?” Like an up-to-date vaudeville team, Xanthias and Dionysus start off a dialogue that mingles wit and poetry with humor and keen satire.

days.title: Poe on Poetry
intro: Regarded in Europe as one of America’s greatest writers, Poe originated the detective story, perfected the mystery short story, and produced America’s first great poems. Here he unravels the fabric of which all poetry is woven.
days.printed: Read from Poe’s The Poetic Principle

days.title: “Ah! It Is St. Agnes’ Eve—”
intro: At midnight on the eve of St. Agnes there were certain solemn ceremonies which all virgins must perform to have “visions of delight and soft adorings from their loves.” Porphyro took advantage of this custom to win his bride.
days.printed: Read: Keats’ Eve of St. Agnes

days.title: The Nightingale’s Healing Melody
intro: The Emperor of China lies on his deathbed grieving for the song of his favorite bird. Hark, the song! It charms, coaxes, and bribes Death to depart. It brings new life to the master.

days.title: A King’s Pleasure Now Yours
intro: The classic plays of French literature are produced to-day precisely as when they were given for the resplendent kings they were written to please. We are fortunate to have in English, excellent translations of these noble plays.
notes: Corneille elected to French Academy, Jan. 22, 1647.

days.title: Pascal Knew Men and Triangles
intro: Pascal, the keen-minded philosopher and mathematician, fathomed the human traits of man’s nature with the same accurate measurements which made him famous in the realm of geometry. Read his searching analysis of man’s conceit.
days.printed: Read: Pascal’s The Art of Persuasion

days.title: Odysseus Silenced the Sirens
intro: When his ship approached the siren’s rock, Odysseus stuffed the ears of his crew with wax and had himself bound to the mast that he might hear the alluring voice of the siren and yet not wreck his ship on the enchanted rock.

days.title: A Field Mouse Made Famous
intro: A humble Scotchman, plowing his fields, turns over the nest of a frightened mouse. He apologizes with the deepest sincerity and explains how “the best-laid schemes o’ mice an’ men gang aft agley.”

readings.author: Robert Burns
readings.work: To a Mouse and Burns’ other poems

readings.author: Robert Burns
readings.work: To a Mouse and Burns’ other poems

days.printed: Read: To a Mouse and Burns’ other poems

days.title: In the Cradle of Civilization
intro: A king who entombed his daughter in a golden cow—the worship of the bull and the cat—scandal of the court and the gossip of the temples is given by Herodotus in his delightful story of old Egypt.
days.printed: Read from Herodotus’ An Account of Egypt

days.title: Dante and Beatrice in Paradise
intro: Dante fell madly in love with Beatrice at first sight; but it is doubted if he ever spoke to her in this world. He tells of his happy meeting with Beatrice in Paradise.
notes: Dante victim of political persecution in Florence, Jan. 27, 1302.

days.title: Man’s Wings
intro: A pure heart, says Thomas à Kempis, comprehends the very depths of Heaven and Hell. And it is by the wings of simplicity and purity that man is lifted above all earthly things.

days.title: Visits the Land of Fire
intro: South of Patagonia is Tierra del Fuego—“The Land of Fire.” The natives of that primitive country are to-day almost extinct. Darwin made a careful and vitally interesting study of that land and its ill-fated inhabitants.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle

days.title: First Problem Play Popular
intro: Antigone, an orphan princess, defies a king’s mandate and risks her life to do her duty to her brother. What is this duty which her brother calls her to perform and the king forbids?
notes: Sophocles died at Athens, Jan. 30, 405 B. C.

days.title: What “Don Quixote” Really Slew
intro: Slayer of windmills, rescuer of fair damsels in distress, eccentric Don Quixote, scores of years behind his time, set out on a mad quest of knight-errantry. Worlds of fun and killing satire are in this absorbing story of Cervantes.

days.title: King Arthur’s Knights Find Holy Grail
intro: The intrepid Knights of the Round Table were startled by “crackling and crying of thunder” which rang through the great hall of the castle. Then there entered “The Holy Grail covered with white samite.”
days.printed: Read from Malory’s The Holy Grail

days.title: “Apparel Oft Proclaims the Man”
intro: Before his son, Laertes, departs for a foreign country, Polonius advises him as to his conduct and dress, while Hamlet, the king’s son, has to learn by experience.

days.title: A House of Mirth and Revelry
intro: While the cat’s away the mice will play. Boisterous and ludicrous happenings occur in a house left in charge of a servant. But in midst of merriment the master returns.
notes: Ben Jonson receives life pension from James I, Feb. 3, 1619.

days.title: “Genius, a Secret to Itself”
intro: Thus wrote Carlyle, who affirms that great minds are unconscious of their stupendous strength. And each of us has his own peculiar mental attributes.

days.title: Diamonds, Diamonds Everywhere!
intro: Trapped in a valley filled with huge diamonds guarded by venomous serpents, Sindibad devised a clever means of escaping with many of the glittering jewels.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: Charles Lamb Suggests To-day’s Reading
intro: “The reluctant pangs of abdicating royalty in ‘Edward’ furnished hints which Shakespeare scarcely improved in his ‘Richard the Second,’ and the death scene of Marlowe’s King moves to pity and terror.”—Charles Lamb.
days.printed: Read from Marlowe’s Edward the Second

days.title: A Letter from a Lion
intro: Johnson was not always a conventional guest. Graciously treated, he responded in like manner, but offended, Johnson could wield a pen dripping with vitriol.
notes: Samuel Johnson writes to Lord Chesterfield, Feb. 7, 1755.

days.title: Tragic Death of a World-Famous Beauty
intro: “But I, the Queen of a’ Scotland, maun lie in prison strang.” Burns sings of poor Mary bound by chains, yearning for the day when flowers would “bloom on her peaceful grave.”
notes: Mary, Queen of Scots, beheaded Feb. 8, 1587.

days.title: Rest Between Wars
intro: Tacitus, the historian, visited the virile German tribes in their primitive homes on the banks of the Rhine. He was surprised to learn that the men so active and eager in war lolled in indolence during the intervals between.

days.title: No Fancy for a Plain Gentleman
intro: Voltaire once visited Congreve. This famous dramatist requested to be regarded only as a plain gentleman. “Had you been that I should never have come to see you,” Voltaire cynically replies.
days.printed: Read from Voltaire’s Letters on the English

days.title: The Queen Freezes Her Philosophy
intro: Descartes was slain through the eccentric whim of a queen who demanded that he tutor her in the freezing dawn in the dead of winter. His philosophy lives in this essay.
days.printed: Read from Descartes’ Discourse on Method
notes: René Descartes died at Stockholm, Feb. 11, 1650.

days.title: Oxford Corrects Lincoln’s Mistake
intro: Lincoln himself thought his famous Gettysburg Address was a failure. To-day the whole world acclaims its greatness. Cast in bronze, it hangs on the wall of Balliol College, Oxford, regarded as the perfection of English prose.

days.title: The Frank Story of an Amazing Life
intro: At the age of fifty-eight Benvenuto Cellini shaved his head and retired to a monastery to write his own story of murder, passion, and great deeds of the Renaissance. His life is a vivid picture of the most colorful period in history, a period when statecraft and religion and black magic and assassination were naïvely mingled in men’s lives.

days.title: Love Always Young
intro: Pascal—an original genius—purposed to master everything that was new in art and science. He was a mathematician and scientist as well as a religious enthusiast and moralist, and he shows a decidedly human side of his nature in this superb essay on Love.

readings.author: Blaise Pascal
readings.work: Pascal’s Discourse on the Passion of Love
readings.title: Discourse on the Passion of Love

days.printed: Read: Pascal’s Discourse on the Passion of Love

days.title: The World Well Lost?
intro: The romantic and heedless loves of Antony and Cleopatra figure prominently in history, literature, and drama. Dryden made a fascinating play from the story of Antony, who sacrificed the leadership of Rome, reputation, and life itself for love of the Egyptian queen, who followed him in death.
days.printed: Read from Dryden’s All for Love
notes: Mark Antony offers Cæsar crown at Rome, Feb. 15, 44 B. C.

days.title: Social Circles Among Ants
intro: Ants have slaves who work for them. These slaves make the nests, feed the master ants, tend the eggs, and do the moving when a colony of ants migrate. Darwin minutely describes the habits and lives of the industrious ants and their marvelous social organization—a wonder to mankind.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Origin of Species

days.title: Death His Curtain Call
intro: While acting in one of his own plays, Molière was suddenly stricken and died shortly after the final curtain. He took an important rôle in “Tartuffe” which introduces to literature a character as famous as Shakespeare’s Falstaff.

days.title: Lasting Peace with Great Britain
intro: All Americans should know this treaty which finally inaugurated an era of peace and good understanding with England. For over a hundred years this peace has been unbroken.
notes: Treaty with Great Britain proclaimed Feb. 18, 1815.

days.title: Earthly Experience of a Chinese Goddess
intro: The thousandth celestial wife of the Garland God slipped and fell to earth, where she took mortal form and served as an attendant in a temple. Death finally released her and she went back to heaven to tell her lord of the ways of men.

days.title: Voltaire Observes the Quakers
intro: Because the early Quakers shook, trembled, and quaked when they became inspired—they received the title of “Quakers.” This sect attracted the keen-minded Voltaire, who made interesting notes on them during his visit to England.
days.printed: Read from Voltaire’s Letters on the English

days.title: Does Football Make a College?
intro: Just what makes a university? A group of fine buildings? A library? A staff of well-trained teachers? A body of eager students? A winning football team? Cardinal Newman defines the prime functions of a university.

readings.author: John Henry Newman
readings.work: Newman’s The Idea of a University
readings.title: The Idea of a University

days.printed: Read from Newman’s The Idea of a University

days.title: An Ode for Washington’s Birthday
intro: Burns asks for Columbia’s harp, and then sings of liberty. He bewails the sad state of the land of Alfred and Wallace which once championed liberty, and now fights for tyranny.

days.title: Pepys’ Nose for News
intro: Gossipy, witty Pepys had a curiosity that made him famous. He knew all the news of court and street. Stevenson, who never put his pen to a dull subject, writes of Pepys.

days.title: Lights and Shadows of Milton
intro: In a superb poem, Milton bids Loathed Melancholy begone to some dark cell. He calls for the joys of youth and vows eternal faith with them.
notes: John Milton marries his third wife, Elizabeth Marshall, Feb. 24, 1662.

days.title: Punished for Too Sharp a Wit
intro: The brilliant wit and cutting satire of Defoe made for him friends and enemies—but mostly enemies. So piercing and two-edged was “The Shortest-Way with Dissenters” that he was fined, imprisoned and pilloried.

days.title: A David Who Side-stepped Goliath
intro: Hugo was insulted by the most powerful critics in France. He put into the preface of a play “his sling and his stone” by which others might slay “the classical Goliath.”

days.title: Poet Apostle of Good Cheer
intro: “Tell me not in mournful numbers, life is but an empty dream . . .” “Stars of the summer night! Far in yon azure deeps—” So begin poems that have charmed and cheered thousands.

days.title: Spoke Latin First
intro: Proficient in Latin even before he knew his own tongue, Montaigne received an unusual education. His whole life was spent in storing up his choice thoughts for our profit and pleasure.

days.title: Goethe’s Tale of a Maiden in Love
intro: To either Saint Patrick or the Scottish Parliament of 1228 go the honors—or dishonors—of originating the traditions attending this day; says the latter, “ilka maiden ladee, of baith high and lowe estait, shall hae libertie to speak ye man she likes.” The course of true love runs smooth in Goethe’s narrative poem, enduring today for its characterization and swift-flowing lines.

days.title: Invented Sir Roger de Coverly
intro: Word pictures are often more vivid than photographs. Steele had a gift for originating characters that are remembered longer than flesh and blood people. Sir Roger de Coverly and Will Honeycomb are now bold figures in literature.
notes: First issue of the “Spectator,” published March 1, 1711.

days.title: What Sailors Do on Sunday
intro: “A sailor’s liberty is but for a day,” as Dana explains. Dressed in his Sunday best, the sailor feels like a dashing Beau Brummel; and sets out to enjoy his freedom. “While it lasts it is perfect. He is under no one’s eye and can do whatever he pleases.”

readings.author: Richard Henry Dana, Jr.
readings.work: Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
readings.title: Two Years Before the Mast

days.printed: Read from Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast

days.title: For Poets and Fishermen
intro: Isaak Walton, famed patron of fishermen, appreciated other arts and hobbies. He writes of George Herbert, a preacher whose hobby was poetry.
days.printed: Read from Walton’s Life of George Herbert

days.title: Penn—Pioneer, Thinker, and Builder
intro: Penn, true to Quaker beliefs, came before the king with his hat on. The king overlooked this and later made him governor of Pennsylvania. A sagacious Penn is revealed in his writings.
days.printed: Read from Penn’s Some Fruits of Solitude
notes: King Charles grants Penn charter of Pennsylvania, March 4, 1681.

days.title: Laughed at Locks
intro: Prison walls were the least of Cellini’s troubles. “Lock me well up and watch me, for I shall certainly contrive to escape.” In spite of this warning, the utmost care of the jailers only furnished amusement for the dauntless Cellini.

days.title: West Point’s Outcast, America’s First Great Poet
intro: Edgar Allan Poe was expelled from West Point and disinherited. So poor was he that when his young wife lay dying, he could not afford a fire to warm her. The weirdness and despair of “The Raven” is particularly symbolic of his life.
notes: Poe expelled from West Point, March 6, 1831.

days.title: Bacon Warns Judges
intro: Bacon pointed out that a judge’s duty was to interpret laws and not to make laws. This single essay of Bacon’s is a richly condensed summary of the ethics of law.
notes: Bacon made Keeper of the Great Seal of England, March 7, 1616.

days.title: Dangerous Experiment with a Wife
intro: Anselmo and Lothario were close friends. Anselmo, anxious to learn if his wife were perfect, as he believed her to be, makes an unusual proposal to his old friend.

days.title: Common Sense and Good Manners
intro: Swift regretted the laws against dueling because dueling at least was a good means of ridding the country of bores and fools. His keen eye penetrated social customs and saw the common sense that governed good manners.
notes: Passage of laws against dueling in England, March 9, 1679.

days.title: Beaumont—The Adonis of Elizabethan Playwrights
intro: In the days when contact with the theatre meant exile from the best society, Beaumont and Fletcher, men from good families, dared to ally themselves with the stage as playwrights. “Philaster” won them immortal praise.

days.title: Gain Gleaned from Suffering
intro: We are paid for our suffering and we pay for our happiness. Every ache, every sorrow receives its recompense here on earth. Emerson gives the basis for this conviction.

days.title: An Irish Bishop’s Wit
intro: Berkeley believed in a great religious future for America. He lived three years in Rhode Island, and made plans for a college in Bermuda.

days.title: Before Nobility Ran Tea Rooms
intro: Manzoni has pictured in this thrilling romance of the seventeenth century nobility, the pompous and sporting life of those good old days when nobles lived sumptuously in spacious castles surrounded by vast estates.
days.printed: Read from Manzoni’s I Promessi Sposi

days.title: A Maiden’s Forfeit
intro: “This gentlewoman that ye lead with you is a maid?” demanded the knight. “Sir,” said she, “a maid I am.” “Then she must yield us the custom of this castle.”
notes: Malory, recorder of King Arthur stories, died March 14, 1470.

days.title: Beware the Ides of March!
intro: Twice warned of the danger that threatened him on the Ides of March, although “the earth rocked and the stars fell and headless men walked in the Forum,” Cæsar goes to the doom awaiting him in the Senate Chamber.

days.title: Crabs Climb Trees?
intro: Many amazing things happen in the Malay jungles. For example, Darwin tells about a crab that climbs trees and walks down the trunks for an occasional bath in a pool.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle

days.title: An Old Irish Legend
intro: An old Irish legend tells how, while St. Patrick was preaching about Paradise and Hell, several of his audience begged to be allowed to investigate the reality of these places. St. Patrick actually satisfied their curiosity.

readings.author: Ernest Renan
readings.work: The Poetry of the Celtic Races

days.printed: Read from The Poetry of the Celtic Races

days.title: New Way to Pay Old Debts
intro: A cunning uncle cheats his worthless nephew out of his fortune. The nephew, laughing stock of his former servants, sets out to retrieve his old position and riches.

readings.author: Philip Massinger
readings.work: A New Way to Pay Old Debts

days.printed: Read from A New Way to Pay Old Debts

days.title: Seeing Old Egypt
intro: The mysterious Egyptian temples, the floating islands, the huge pyramids and the many wonders of ancient Egypt are pictured for you by Herodotus.
days.printed: Read from Herodotus’ An Account of Egypt
notes: Last recorded event in Herodotus’ history dated March 19, 478 B. C.

days.title: Apples, Feathers, and Coals
intro: Sir Isaac Newton was aided in his momentous discoveries by the most insignificant objects—even apples, feathers, and coal. Voltaire discusses the wondrous discoveries of Newton.
days.printed: Read from Voltaire’s Letters on the English

days.title: 1,000 Years of History on the Surface of a Shield
intro: Venus, mother of Æneas and wife of Vulcan, obtained from her husband, by seductive witchery, a marvelous shield whose surface reflected a thousand years of future events. Venus describes the wonders of the magic armor.

days.title: From Puppet Show to Majestic Drama
intro: The Faust legend, which can be traced to puppet shows of earlier days, portrays a philosopher who, through Satan’s aid and in return for the price of his soul, works magic at will. From this rude framework Goethe has reared a drama of sublime grandeur.

days.title: First of a Thousand Harem Stories
intro: Shahrazad, favorite of the treacherous Sultan’s harem, selected a most thrilling story for her bridal night. By leaving it unfinished she was privileged to live to continue it the next night—and so on for a thousand and one nights.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: A Queen Pleads
intro: Guenevere, King Arthur’s queen, justly accused but harshly treated, makes a noble and brave attempt to convince her court that Gawaine lied and that Launcelot was true.

days.title: How Conscience Makes Cowards of Us All
intro: Hamlet pondered over which course contained the least unhappiness—whether to suffer here and not incur new dangers, or whether to end it all and chance the unknown terrors of the next world. See how Hamlet reasoned.

days.title: “2,500 Years Ago Æsop Said . . .”
intro: Men in all ages have recognized the ingenuity of the practical philosophy and freshness of Æsop’s allegories. Spend a few delightful moments with the wit and wisdom of Æsop.

days.title: When Is a Lie Not a Lie?
intro: Is lying or quibbling ever permissible? May one juggle words so a truth is conveyed through a lie and a lie told by a truth? Stevenson unravels this puzzle.

days.title: Pins and Other Points
intro: The making of a simple pin is one of the most complex affairs of modern industry. Adam Smith regards the process from the worker’s point of view, and shows the many and varied economic principles that are involved in pin making.
days.printed: Read from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations

days.title: Hero and Goddess Break Engagement
intro: Brynhild, favorite goddess of Norse mythology, plighted troth with Sigurd, fearless warrior. But Sigurd forgot Brynhild and married Gudrun, whose brother, Gunner, then set out to win the beautiful Brynhild. Complications very like a modern triangle arose.

days.title: The Plague of Milan
intro: “I Promessi Sposi,” a seventeenth century novel, vividly describes the devastating plague of Milan. Then whole families sickened in a few hours and died in less than a day’s time of strange and violent complaints whose symptoms were unknown to physicians.
days.printed: Read from Manzoni’s I Promessi Sposi
notes: Capuchin monks given charge of the plague hospital in Milan, March 30, 1630.

days.title: The Ghastly Whim of John Donne
intro: Monuments are usually made from death masks, but John Donne took pleasure in posing for his, wrapped from head to foot in a shroud. Isaak Walton tells of this in his fascinating biography of the eccentric poet.
days.printed: Read from Walton’s Life of Dr. Donne

days.title: “Oh! to Be in England Now That April’s There”
intro: Everyone knows the pangs of homesickness in the spring. Even bright, sparkling Italy could not wean Browning’s affection from the green hedgerows of misty England.

days.title: A Spoon Dances in the Moonlight
intro: A huge spoon dressed in human finery, placed on a grave, appears to become convulsed when the moon’s rays fall on it and dances to the tune of chanting natives. Weird sights, according to Darwin, abound in the South Seas.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle

days.title: Romance with a Happy Ending
intro: “As a conqueror enters a surprised city; love made such resolutions as neither party was able to resist. She changed her name into Herbert the third day after this first interview.”
days.printed: Read from Walton’s Life of George Herbert

days.title: The Mistakes of a Night
intro: Genial and rollicking fun are provided in this highly entertaining story of a man who mistakes a private house for an inn, and who treats his host’s daughter like a serving maid.
days.printed: Read from She Stoops to Conquer

days.title: You and Your Dreams
intro: Dreams and their causes interested Hobbes. Without superstition, the philosopher weighed the evidence of ghosts, goblins, and witches.

days.title: Who Is Bad?
intro: Badness has many interpretations, a different definition has been the dictate of each new generation. The solution of the eternal riddle was earnestly sought by Marcus Aurelius.
notes: Marcus Aurelius born April 6, 121 A. D.

days.title: Nature Guided His Pen
intro: Wordsworth was so closely in touch with Nature that the simple beauty of flowers, woods, and fields is reflected in his poems as if Nature herself took up the pen and wrote.

days.title: Beware the Vengeful Hounds!
intro: Orestes, holding an avenging sword over his mother, is told: “Beware thy mother’s vengeful hounds.” How he pays for disregarding his mother’s warning is told in this drama where a mother is slain to avenge a father’s ghost.
days.printed: Read from Æschylus’ The Libation Bearers

days.title: A Perfect Land in a Wilderness of Waters
intro: West of Peru there was reported to be a land where Truth and Science were used to promote the happiness and freedom of man. Here is Bacon’s description of this ideal commonwealth.

days.title: Americans—by Will of the King
intro: Before English adventurers could attempt settlement in America it was necessary first to get permission from the King. The charter of King James to the oldest American colony is an extremely important historical document.
notes: King James grants charter to Virginia, April 10, 1606.

days.title: Danger in Being Young and Fair
intro: The virgin beauty of Margaret enchanted Faust, who dazzled her with the brilliance of many gems. Margaret innocently took his gifts, believing that beauty should not “blush unseen”—but unmindful of consequences to follow.

days.title: The Perfect Argument
intro: You would doubtless like to know how to hold your own in any argument. Read what Leslie Stephen declares the finest specimen in our language of the conduct of argument.

days.title: Michelangelo His Boon Companion
intro: Kings, emperors, the greatest artists and sculptors of the Renaissance at its most magnificent period, walk through the pages of his autobiography—not as cold, austere, historical character, but as the intimate friends of Cellini.

days.title: A Raid on Spanish Treasure in America
intro: Spanish towns in the New World were rich in treasure and tempting booty for English soldiers of fortune, who were venturesome and merciless. “Ho! for the Spanish Main!” was the rallying cry for all freebooters and buccaneers.
days.printed: Read from Biggs’ Drake’s Great Armada

days.title: O Captain! My Captain!
intro: The rugged, genuine Lincoln was idealized by Walt Whitman—the founder of the new school of American poetry. Two of Whitman’s finest poems were inspired by Lincoln.

days.title: Inside the Gates of Hell
intro: The city of Dis, within the gates of Hell, was guarded by monsters and surrounded by a moat filled with the tormented. Dante, protected by Virgil, entered the forbidden city, and viewed sights never before seen by living man.
notes: Dante urges attack on the city of Florence, April 16, 1311.

days.title: Benjamin Franklin—Book Salesman
intro: In 1731 there were not many books in America. Franklin saw the need for more books and by house-to-house canvassing persuaded Philadelphians to aid him in founding a public library which to-day stands as a lasting memorial to Franklin.

days.title: Ready for Adventures and Conquests
intro: Reading too many romances of knights and valorous deeds caused a poor Spanish gentleman to polish up his great-grandfather’s armor, rechristen his old nag, and sally forth. “Don Quixote,” besides holding a secure niche in literature as the work that quashed the romantic school of knight-errantry, is at the same time one of the most widely-read stories in the world.
notes: Cervantes receives the last sacraments April 18, 1616.

days.title: Battle of Concord
intro: Dr. Eliot says of the opening stanza of the “Concord Hymn”: “In twenty-eight words here are the whole scene and all the essential circumstances . . . what an accurate, moving, immortal description is this!”

days.title: Byron Gave His Life for Freedom
intro: England’s romantic poet died while fighting against the Turks on the side of the Greeks. His poems, “The Isles of Greece” and “The Prisoner of Chillon,” proclaim freedom.
notes: At Missolonghi, Greece, 37 guns honor Byron, April 20, 1824.

days.title: Books as Windows to the Past
intro: Through the pages of a book the reader sees the life of past days. Carnivals, processions, battles, coronations, voyages—the whole history of the world and its people is revealed in a stupendous pageant. Taine was a Frenchman who wrote an unsurpassed history of English literature; its introduction reveals the unusual combination of an imaginative and an analytical style.
days.printed: Read from Introduction to English Literature

days.title: Happiness as a Duty
intro: Immanuel Kant, the most influential of German philosophers, taught that it was man’s duty to be happy, for an unhappy man is tempted to sin. Seekers after happiness find aid and inspiration in Kant’s writings.
days.printed: Read from Fundamental Principles of Morals

days.title: “If You Have Poison for Me, I Will Drink It”
intro: Shaken and disillusioned by the treachery of his elder daughter, King Lear suspected even the faithful Cordelia of evil designs. Her most tender efforts to comfort him failed to drive away the insistent specter of his madness.

days.title: Nineteen Million Elephants
intro: At the rate at which elephants naturally increase, Darwin estimated that in 750 years there could be nearly 19,000,000 elephants. But did Darwin consider the ravages of civilization and circuses?
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Origin of Species

days.title: Mighty Rome Feared These Men
intro: Men who danced among sharp swords—who gambled with their lives—who took their women to the battlefields to encourage the brave and shame the cowardly—these were the primitive Germans who made Roman emperors tremble.

days.title: Do Miracles Still Happen
intro: Just what constitutes a miracle? Does Science indorse miracles? One wonders why such marvelous things do not happen often nowadays. Hume tells why.

days.title: He Dared to See Forbidden Beauty
intro: The Puritan world feared Beauty. Emerson, great American essayist and philosopher, declared that the world was made for beauty, and openly worshiped at beauty’s shrine.

days.title: “Vanity of Vanities,” Saith the Preacher
intro: Three hundred years before Christ, a preacher in Jerusalem complained that there was no new thing under the sun. Everything considered new had really existed in the time of the fathers. Sophisticated and modern is this writer of 2,300 years ago.
days.printed: Read from The Book of Ecclesiastes

days.title: How I Got Rich—by Sindbad the Sailor
intro: Sindbad, a poor man, recited woeful verses before the magnificent dwelling of Sindbad of the Sea. The great Sindbad, hearing him, invited the poor Sindbad to a feast and told the wonderful story of his fabulous fortune.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: Washington’s Dictum on Private Life
intro: Washington declared that the strength of the new nation lay in the “pure and immutable principles of private morality.” A free government, fortified by the virtues and affection of its citizens, can command the respect of the world.

days.title: What Would You Ask Judas Iscariot?
intro: Once Hazlitt and his friends took to discussing the famous people they would like to meet—Guy Fawkes, Sir Isaac Newton, Chaucer, Boccaccio, Cromwell, Garrick, and Judas.

readings.author: William Hazlitt
readings.work: Persons One Would Wish to Have Seen

days.printed: Read: Persons One Would Wish to Have Seen

days.title: First Sparks of Electricity
intro: Everything has to have a beginning, so too with the science of electricity. Here we learn the very rudiments, the inceptions of science that have revolutionized the world. Faraday explains in a simple way the truths of electricity.

days.title: Why “Machiavellian”?
intro: Traveling from court to court in the stirring days of the Renaissance, Machiavelli studied the intrigues of princes. His writings have affected the destiny of mighty dynasties.

days.title: A Champion of Science
intro: When science was struggling for a place in popular education, Huxley distinguished himself as its champion. While the arts were to beautify life and increase pleasure, Huxley saw science as a means of benefiting man’s prosperity.

days.title: Strange Adventures in Man’s Clothes
intro: Disguised as a man, a Russian noblewoman exploring the mountains of Poland came upon a secret prison. Fate linked the lives of this woman and the unknown prisoner.
days.printed: Read from Calderon’s Life Is a Dream
notes: Calderon, after a life of adventure, died May 5, 1681.

days.title: A Poor Artist Defies a Rich Duke
intro: “Benvenuto, the figure cannot succeed in bronze,” so spoke the patron Duke. Cellini, stung to fury, passionately burst out: “You do not understand art.” Feverishly he began the casting of the statue—but read his own account of the tilt with the Duke.

days.title: A Bishop Bargains
intro: A haughty aristocrat, who murdered his wife for enjoying life more than he, now bargaining for a new bride; a crafty bishop begging and bullying his heirs for a tomb richer than that of his rival; these are subjects of Browning’s pen.

days.title: Behind the Screen in the School for Scandal
intro: Lady Teazle hides in haste when her husband is unexpectedly announced. Situations which set many tongues wagging and fed the fire of gossip in Scandal-land, startle the reader.
days.printed: Read from Sheridan’s School for Scandal
notes: “School for Scandal” produced at Drury Lane, May 8, 1777.

days.title: Relation of Art to Freedom
intro: Who has ever thought the arts had anything to do with freedom? Schiller did. Forced by a German noble to enter a military school, he escaped. Struggling to achieve freedom, he wrote a series of letters on the relation of art to freedom.

days.title: A Knight Among Cannibals
intro: Savages who drink the powdered bones of their dead mixed with wine, Amazons who hold riotous festivals, the worship of golden statues, all the primitive wonders of Guiana are described by the famous Elizabethan gallant, Sir Walter Raleigh.
days.printed: Read from Raleigh’s Discovery of Guiana

days.title: Latest Gossip in Malfi
intro: Latest news abroad in Malfi: The Duchess has run off with her butler. But this happened before the days of newspapers or radio, so Webster made from it an exciting play.
days.printed: Read from Webster’s The Duchess of Malfi

days.title: His Wife’s Golden Hair Enshrined His Poems
intro: The manuscripts of many of the best poems of Rossetti were buried with his wife. Friends prevailed upon him to allow them to be exhumed—and these poems, once buried with the dead, are now a treasure of the living.

days.title: What Does Your Dog Think of You?
intro: Two dogs fell a-gossiping about their masters and about a dog’s life among the humble Scotch folk. Each “rejoic’d they werena men but dogs; an’ each took aff his several way.”

days.title: Jenner’s Amazing Smallpox Cure
intro: Edward Jenner found that disease in the heel of a horse, transmitted through a cow to the dairy attendants, was an agent in making human beings immune from smallpox. His amazing experiments inaugurated a new epoch.
notes: Edward Jenner makes his first vaccination May 14, 1796.

days.title: Glimpses Into the Beyond
intro: The best part of the Divine Comedy for a few minutes’ reading is the “Inferno.” There the reader finds the most vivid descriptions, the most startling and unforgettable pictures.

days.title: Favorite Superstitions of Celtic Imagination
intro: Chessboards on which, of their own accord, black pieces played against white; chariots that swiftly turned hither and yon without a driver; pots in which a coward’s meat would not cook—all these are woven into bewitching stories.

readings.author: Ernest Renan
readings.work: The Poetry of the Celtic Races

days.printed: Read from The Poetry of the Celtic Races

days.title: An Honest Life’s Reward
intro: Condemned for impiety, Socrates felt so justified in the virtue of his past action that instead of receiving a death sentence, he told the judges he should be maintained at public expense as a public benefactor.

days.title: The Night Life of Flowers
intro: Flowers often tire of their stationary life and sometimes at night frolic away to a ball in a beautiful castle. Thus a fanciful storyteller accounts for their drooping condition in the morning.

days.title: Golden Advice on Manners
intro: When a man is invited to a banquet he must be satisfied with the dishes put before him. Epictetus reasoned that man should be content with what life offers, and in serenity find happiness.

days.title: Shakespeare’s Finest Work
intro: The most concentrated beauty of Shakespeare’s unbounded creative genius is found in his sonnets. Written as personal messages to friends and not intended for publication, they reveal the inner Shakespeare more truly than do any of his great plays.
notes: Sonnets entered in the London Stationers’ Register, May 20. 1609.

days.title: An Honest Man Defined
intro: The sharp tongue of Alexander Pope made him celebrated, yet widely feared. In a representative product of his versatile pen, he gracefully combines his flashing wit with sage advice.
days.printed: Read from Pope’s Essay on Man

days.title: True Love in Difficulty
intro: Because of a fancy for a peasant girl, the tyrannical lord of an Italian village sent desperadoes to threaten the priest if he married the girl to her village lover.
days.printed: Read from Manzoni’s I Promessi Sposi

days.title: A Plea for an Unfortunate
intro: From the river her body was tenderly lifted—the girl who could find no place in the vast city. Thomas Hood pleads for her—eloquently and justly. Read this gem of pathos.

days.title: They Had No Money—Yet Bought and Sold
intro: Debts were not always paid in money. Not so long ago the butcher paid for his keg of beer with a slab of beef, and oxen were exchanged for land and wives. Adam Smith tells the interesting story of the origin and use of money.
days.printed: Read from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations

days.title: Do What You Fear
intro: Emerson startled the world by fearlessly declaring his beliefs. Such apparent paradoxes as we find in his inspirational essay, “Heroism,” makes him the most stimulating yet profound thinker America has produced.

days.title: Daughter Declares Her Love
intro: Goneril and Regan falsely swore they loved their father, King Lear, more than life itself. Cordelia could find no words to express her sincere devotion. Then King Lear made the decision that started a series of exciting events.
notes: Shakespeare’s first daughter, Susanna, baptized May 26, 1583.

days.title: Lessing’s Courageous Stand for Toleration
intro: To advance freedom of thought, Lessing published an essay of one hundred paragraphs outlining the history of religion. The wrath of orthodox churchmen was hurled at his head, and Lessing was left alone to defend his daring theories.

readings.author: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing
readings.work: The Education of the Human Race

days.printed: Read from The Education of the Human Race

days.title: Master of Melodious Lyrics
intro: Any one of these poems, “The Harp That Once Through Tara’s Halls,” “The Last Rose of Summer,” “The Light of Other Days,” would alone have made Moore immortal.

days.title: Adventures in Bagdad
intro: A Bagdad merchant dreamed of the money he would make from the sale of a tray of glassware, and of marrying the king’s daughter. But, daydreaming, he kicked over the tray.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: When the Throb of the War Drum Is Stifl’d
intro: At the close of the war, a torn and bleeding nation set about to rebuild its shattered frame. The result was a stronger nation rising from an almost disrupted union.

readings.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
readings.work: Longfellow’s The Building of the Ship
readings.title: The Building of the Ship

days.printed: Read: Longfellow’s The Building of the Ship

days.title: America’s Most Surprising Poet
intro: Walt Whitman is the most original and startling of modern poets. An irony of his life is that while he wrote for the contemporary masses, only a limited number of followers appreciated his genius, now universally recognized.

readings.author: Walt Whitman
readings.work: Whitman’s Preface to Leaves of Grass
readings.title: Preface to Leaves of Grass

days.printed: Read: Whitman’s Preface to Leaves of Grass

days.title: Thrilling Play by Tutor of Shakespeare
intro: For the best blank verse in English, read “Dr. Faustus,” the masterpiece of Marlowe, who gave Shakespeare lessons in playwriting. This genius knew the secret of gripping drama.

days.title: “Back to Nature” in the Seventeenth Century
intro: A “Back to Nature” movement in the seventeenth century was headed by Rousseau, who believed that civilization was degrading. To save money for his work, he entrusted each of his children to the tender mercies of a foundling house.
days.printed: Read from Rousseau’s A Savoyard Vicar

days.title: Pulse Aids Epochal Discoveries
intro: Galileo, by holding his pulse while watching a swinging cathedral lamp, evolved a theory that made clocks possible. Harvey, by feeling his pulse, educed that arteries carry blood.

readings.author: William Harvey
readings.work: Motion of the Heart and Blood

days.printed: Read from Motion of the Heart and Blood

days.title: ’Neath the Iron Hand of Spain
intro: Spain sent the Duke of Alva to subdue the Netherlands. In quelling disorder he killed the people’s hero, Count Egmont. From this story Goethe made a famous play.

days.title: The Rent of Land from Human Food
intro: Even to-day rent is paid in terms of human food. It sounds primitive, but it happens right at your door—here in the United States, in compliance with a law as old as man.
days.printed: Read from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations

days.title: A Shrill Cry in the Night!
intro: A crew faced the hazardous prospect of rounding the bleak Cape Horn in midwinter. Imagine the terror when a sudden scream pierced the misery-laden air. What was it? A man overboard or a lost soul?

readings.author: Richard Henry Dana, Jr.
readings.work: Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
readings.title: Two Years Before the Mast

days.printed: Read from Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
notes: R. H. Dana on watch, night of June 6, 1836.

days.title: “There’s Rosemary—that’s for Remembrance!”
intro: Do you know the rest of Ophelia’s famous line? “Hamlet” is the most popular play in the entire world. It has been quoted so often that reading it is like meeting an old friend.
notes: Edwin Booth, famed Shakespearian actor, died June 7, 1893.

days.title: Eloquence Wins Over Prejudice
intro: The plain, homely appearance of Woolman impressed unfavorably the orthodox Quakers in London whom he was sent to meet. They told him his coming was not necessary. But Woolman spoke with such simplicity and sincerity that even those most opposed became his friends.
notes: John Woolman arrives in London for Friends’ meeting, June 8, 1772.

days.title: Enchanting Songs of David
intro: The songs of David pleased King Saul, but when David became too popular with the people, the king feared for his throne and banished him.

days.title: Horrible Prophecy Fulfilled
intro: King Œdipus of Thebes as a babe was abandoned on Mount Cithæron to die. Years after he was thought dead he returns to Thebes and unknowingly slays his father, marries his mother—and thus fulfills the word of the oracle.
days.printed: Read from Sophocles’ Œdipus, King of Thebes

days.title: He Sang of His Beautiful Elizabeth
intro: To commemorate his marriage to the beautiful Elizabeth, Spenser wrote one of the most enchanting nuptial hymns.
notes: Edmund Spenser married Elizabeth Boyle, June 11, 1594.

days.title: Vishnu Holds Up a Battle
intro: Two armies of ancient India were about to engage in a momentous battle. Arjuna, heroic leader of the Pandu hosts, foreseeing great slaughter, hesitates. He implores the divine Vishnu to intervene. The conversation of the warrior and the god is a gem of Hindu literature.

days.title: Athens Flouts Aristides
intro: Athenians gave Aristides the title of “The Just.” Later they wanted to banish him. One voter wanted Aristides banished merely because he was weary of hearing him called “The Just.”

days.title: A Philosopher Prefers Prison Cell
intro: Socrates unceasingly strove for beauty, truth, and perfection. Sentenced to death on a false charge, he refused to escape from the death cell, even when opportunity was offered.

days.title: Strikers Storm the Tower of London
intro: Led by Wat Tyler in 1381, great troops of villagers and rustics marched on London—laid siege to the Tower—sacked the apartments of the King and murdered his ministers. Froissart gives first-hand information of this rebellion.
days.printed: Read from Froissart’s Wat Tyler’s Rebellion

days.title: Spirits at the Top of the World
intro: The inaccessible mountain tops were ever venerated as the haunts of all mysteries. Manfred, hero of Byron’s play, seeks upon the high Alps the aid of spirits, specters, and goblins. What unearthly adventures await him!

days.title: Risked His Scalp in Prayer
intro: John Eliot put his life at the mercy of the redmen to get them to listen to his preachings. He wrote vividly about his settlements of Christian Indians. Now villages and Indians have disappeared. Only his story remains.
notes: John Eliot holds Indian prayer meeting June 17, 1670.

days.title: Cinderella Lives To-day
intro: Cinderella inspires all alike—the artist’s brush, the author’s pen, the child’s fancy. To-day she is a living, vital character to be seen on stage and screen. No one ever forgets her lightning change.

days.title: Freaks of the Dog Fad in England
intro: A writer of Elizabethan times said that no other country had as many dogs as England. Once Henry VII ordered all mastiffs to be hung because they “durst presume to fight against the lion,” England’s regal beast.

days.title: No Salt for These Birds
intro: Galapagos Islands are the home of fearless birds, to which horses, cows, and men are only roosting places. Darwin saw the South Pacific when few travelers knew that wonderland.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle

days.title: Would You Converse with Royalty?
intro: Why gossip with lesser persons when you might be talking to queens and kings? Just how we may get to talk to queens and kings, Ruskin delightfully points out and escorts us to the very doors of the audience chamber.

days.title: Pliny Tells Ghost Stories
intro: Pliny, who lived in the first century after Christ, tells of a ghost who dragged his jangling chains through a house in Athens and so terrified the inmates that they fled panic-stricken. But the ghost met his equal.

days.title: Greek Scholar at Three
intro: John Stuart Mill—one of the greatest intellects in England—tells how his father educated him. At the early age of three years he began the study of Greek, and at twelve started writing a book of his own.
notes: James Mill, father of John Stuart Mill, died June 23, 1836.

days.title: Had No Right Hand
intro: A handsome young man was seen to eat only with his left hand, which was contrary to the customs of Arabia. The youth, when urged, told why he used only his left hand, and revealed a story of love and adventure and the lover’s need for gold—all happening in ancient Cairo.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: Advice to Virgins from a Wise Man
intro: “Gather ye rosebuds while ye may, Old Time is still a-flying; And this same flower that smiles today, to-morrow will be dying?” Herrick was only a humble country minister with a wealth of wisdom and a keen appreciation of life, which he expressed in lyrics of wonderful beauty and melody.

days.title: In the Lair of the Green-Eyed Monster
intro: At the bottom of the ocean was the home of the monster who had desolated the king’s halls. Beowulf, bravest of warriors, descended beneath the waves to fight the beast. The king’s men, waiting above, saw the waves become colored with blood. Hero or monster—who had won?

days.title: Do You Take Poison Daily?
intro: There is a human trait most poisonous to a man’s blood. Man seeks to avoid it because he knows that it lies like a curse upon him. Just what is the poisonous human failing? Who are most subject to it? Bacon tells you in one of his best essays.
notes: Francis Bacon enrolled at Cambridge University, June 27, 1576.

days.title: Pages from the Pampas Book of Etiquette
intro: A very definite etiquette is followed by a stranger on the vast plains of South America. “Ave Maria” is the common salutation. If the stranger is on horseback, he does not alight until invited to do so by his host. Once in the house, the stranger must converse a while before asking shelter for the night.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle

days.title: “Is That a Dagger I See Before Me?”
intro: Macbeth, spurred on by the ambitious and crafty Lady Macbeth, committed murder to secure the crown of Scotland. But he paid dearly for his gain. Ghostly guests appeared at his banquet and threatened him with dire threats.

days.title: Rather King Than Majority
intro: “Democracy” has not always been the choice of oppressed people. The tyranny of the majority is a recognized evil as harmful as the misrule of a king. And rather than exchange a lesser evil for a greater, a rule by king has often been preferred to a republic.

days.title: Darwin Not First Evolutionist
intro: While Darwin was working on his theory of evolution, another scientist independently arrived at the same conclusions. Darwin, then, was not the first to study evolution.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Origin of Species
notes: Darwin publishes outline of “Origin of Species,” July 1, 1858.

days.title: “Julius” Becomes “July”
intro: So that the date for certain festivals would not fall one year in midwinter and in the heat of summer another year, Cæsar reformed the calendar. July was named for him.

days.title: Gettysburg by an Eyewitness
intro: An officer in that momentous battle narrates every major action of both armies. Thus we see the swarming lines of Confederates advance—the hand-to-hand struggle.
days.printed: Read from Haskell’s Battle of Gettysburg

days.title: Some Chose to Remain British Subjects
intro: Some Americans preferred to be loyal to England and did not want independent government. Their hesitation is better understood when the finality of the Declaration is realized.

days.title: A Tailor Entertains a King
intro: Here is another of those fanciful Oriental stories that proclaims the democracy of Eastern despotism. A tailor might talk with a king and receive either a death sentence or the office of Grand Vizier as a reward.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: The Origin of “Utopia”
intro: When Europe was suffering from evil rulers, heavy taxes, and despair, Sir Thomas More dreamed of a happy land where an intelligently managed state perfected happiness.

days.title: Scandal That Lurked Behind Lace and Powder
intro: The painted lips of the eighteenth century ladies and gallants vied with one another in whispering scathing gossip, in gleefully furthering the destruction of a good name. Sheridan depicts this gay world with a brilliant spicy pen.
days.printed: Read from Sheridan’s School for Scandal
notes: Sheridan buried in Westminster Abbey, July 7, 1816.

days.title: Italy’s Fair Assassin
intro: When the monstrous Cenci forced his daughter Beatrice into a horrible situation, she revolted and boldly struck for freedom. Shelley tells her pitiful story in one of his best works.

days.title: A Little Lying Now and Then
intro: “What is Truth?” asked Pilate. For an answer Bacon discourses not on human nature as it should be, but as it is. These shrewd observations on making a life and a living admit occasional departures from truth.

days.title: America’s First Immigrants
intro: The shadow of a phantom cast upon the cradle of Snorri, the first white child born in America, was a warning of an Indian attack on the settlement of courageous Norsemen who had risked the terrors of unknown seas to visit “Wineland.”
days.printed: Read from The Voyages to Vinland

days.title: Star Gazing—A Cure for Tired Minds
intro: The greatest spectacle offered man is a view of the magnificent vault of heaven. Under the stupendous arch of the Milky Way the cares of the world roll off.

readings.author: Simon Newcomb
readings.work: Newcomb’s The Extent of the Universe
readings.title: The Extent of the Universe

days.printed: Read: Newcomb’s The Extent of the Universe

days.title: But He Walked!
intro: Thoreau’s individuality was unique and original. He had no profession; he never married; he never went to church; he never voted or paid taxes; he never smoked; he never drank wine. His amusement was walking, to observe and meditate.

days.title: Athenians Also Complained of Taxes
intro: Pericles used public money to beautify Athens. The citizens protested against the expense, as citizens in all ages do. By a clever stroke Pericles won their support to his ambitious plans.

days.title: The French People Triumph
intro: What the Fourth of July is to Americans, the Fourteenth of July is to Frenchmen. It commemorates an oppressive tyranny overthrown by a freedom-loving people.
days.printed: Read from Burke’s The Revolution in France

days.title: When Elizabeth Dined
intro: Meals in the houses of the gentry and noblemen in Elizabethan England were taken most seriously. No one spoke. Holinshed records the strange table etiquette of our ancestors.
notes: Queen Elizabeth entertained at Kenilworth, July 15, 1575.

days.title: The Mohammedan Jesus
intro: The sacred book of the Moslems, the Koran, gives an account of the birth of Christ. The Koran gives Jesus a high position among the prophets but holds the first place for Mohammed.
notes: Beginning of Moslem era of time, July 16, 622 A. D.

days.title: A Throne for Son or Stepson?
intro: Phædre first persecuted Hippolytus, her handsome stepson, then loved him. Suddenly he and her own son became rivals for the throne. Should she push her son’s claims or let Hippolytus take the crown?
notes: Racine elected to French Academy, July 17, 1673.

days.title: They Loved in Vain
intro: “Browning’s play has thrown me into a perfect passion of sorrow,” wrote Charles Dickens of “The Blot in the ’Scutcheon.” Like Shakespeare’s Juliet, Browning’s Mildred plays the rôle of a youthful lover in a tragic drama.
days.printed: Read from Browning’s Blot in the ’Scutcheon

days.title: She Wanted Heroes All to Herself
intro: The famous gallant who spread his gorgeous cloak so the dainty slipper of his queen would be unspotted, soon lost the high favor this action won for him. In spite of his glorious voyages, Raleigh condemned himself when he fell in love with another woman.
days.printed: Read from Raleigh’s Discovery of Guiana

days.title: A Cobbler in Jail
intro: John Bunyan, imprisoned for preaching without a license, gave to the world “Pilgrim’s Progress,” the greatest allegory in any language, second only to the Bible.

days.title: Scotland’s Own Poet
intro: The songs of Burns are the links, the watchwords, the symbols of the Scots. He is the last of the ballad singers. In his works are preserved the best songs of his people.

days.title: Trapped in a Cave with a Frenzied Giant
intro: Odysseus was wrecked with his men on an island inhabited by one-eyed giants. Trapped in the cave of a giant who gobbled up some of the crew for supper, the cunning Odysseus blinded the giant and rescued the survivors of his crew.

days.title: Friendship Above Love?
intro: There are styles in friendship as well as in clothes. The mode of friendship of Bacon’s time went out with plumed hats and long hose. But Bacon knew the true test of a friend.

days.title: Indian Sorcery Blamed for an Earthquake
intro: Darwin visited a South American city ruined by an earthquake. There he heard the superstitious account of the phenomenon. The ignorant people accused Indian women of bewitching the volcano. But Darwin has another explanation.

readings.author: Charles Darwin
readings.work: Darwin’s The Voyage of the Beagle
readings.title: The Voyage of the Beagle

days.printed: Read from Darwin’s The Voyage of the Beagle

days.title: A Goddess and Her Mortal Lover
intro: Brynhild, Woden’s daughter, carried the dead heroes to Valhalla where they could feast and fight without dying; until a sin divested her of divinity, and she fell in love with Sigurd.

days.title: Peace Amid Strife
intro: While Europe was shaken with wars, Thomas à Kempis lived in happy seclusion in his convent. His writings convincingly reflect the serenity and happiness of a man who has found peace—a peace that surpasses all understanding.

days.title: Once Surgeons Operated in Frock Coats
intro: The use of antiseptics in surgery is new. Hardly more than a half century ago surgeons operated in frock coats. Lord Lister, surgeon to Queen Victoria, was among the first to advocate scrupulous cleanliness in dressing wounds.
notes: Lister publishes paper on antiseptic treatment, July 27, 1867.

days.title: An Idyl of Agriculture
intro: Cowley portrays the ideal life—that of a farmer, and blazons it forth in heraldry. “A plow in a field arable”—to him, the most honorable of all emblems.

days.title: Stonehenge—England’s Unsolved Mystery
intro: Stonehenge, that group of huge, rudely architectural stones on a vast plain in England, was erected no man knows when, nor why, nor how. Emerson, America’s greatest thinker, visited this monument and was amazed at the “uncanny stones.”

days.title: The First English Colony in North America
intro: When the whole coast of America north of Florida was free to the first comer, Sir Humphrey Gilbert naïvely chose to settle on the rugged shores of Newfoundland. Read the glowing account of his great adventure “to plant Christian inhabitants in places convenient.”
notes: Gilbert lands at Newfoundland near St. John’s, July 30, 1583.

days.title: Charm School for Women
intro: Lack of education, writes Defoe, makes a woman “turbulent, clamorous, noisy—” Defoe defied his generation and preached equal education for women. To-day we have co-education, but have we the benefits Defoe predicted?
notes: Defoe pilloried for defiance of public opinion, July 31, 1703.

days.title: His Influence Still Lives
intro: Steadfast allegiance to duty, simple living and adherence to plain, honest, homely doctrines are Calvin’s principles. Are not these same old-fashioned truths followed to-day?

days.title: Poems from a Heart of Love
intro: “Here is the pleasant place—and nothing wanting is, save She, alas!” How often we too are faced with like adversity. So sings Drummond—a master songster and composer.

days.title: When the Greeks Sacked Troy
intro: They battered down the palace gates and ravaged with fire and sword the chambers of King Priam’s hundred wives. Through halls resounding with shrieks of terror, Priam and his household fled to sanctuary.

days.title: World’s Greatest Bedtime Stories
intro: Hans Christian Andersen had an extraordinary capacity for amusing children. Were he living to-day he might be in great demand as a radio bedtime story man.

days.title: Joys of the Simple Life
intro: “Cotter’s Saturday Night” for generations to come will remain the choicest picture of Scotch home life. Into this poem Burns instills the sense of all-pervading peace and happiness that comes at the end of a well-spent day.
notes: Robert Burns married Jean Armour, Aug. 5, 1788.

days.title: A Prophet of Aerial Warfare
intro: “For I dipt into the future—saw the nation’s airy navies grappling in the central blue.” We are amazed at the accuracy of Tennyson’s prediction. But he also foretells “the federation of the world”—yet to be fulfilled.

days.title: The Last Golden Words of Socrates
intro: The death sentence of Socrates could not be executed until the return of the sacred ship from Delos. One day his friends learned that the ship had returned. They hastened to the prison to listen to the last words of Athens’ sage.

days.title: Men Transformed by Circe’s Wand
intro: Unfavorable winds sent by angry gods blew the ships of Odysseus far off their course. The sailors were cast upon a remote island, governed by an enchantress where, for their coarse manners, they were put under a magic spell.

days.title: English Bridal Party Jailed
intro: Minister and witness, bride and groom were arrested by an enraged father when John Donne married his employer’s niece. Donne was soon released, but he found himself without money, position or bride.
days.printed: Read from Walton’s Life of Dr. Donne

days.title: “Give Them Cake,” said the Queen
intro: When the people of Paris howled because they had no bread to eat, Queen Marie Antoinette exclaimed: “Well, then, let them eat cake!” Such an attitude hastened the revolution.
days.printed: Read from Burke’s The Revolution in France

days.title: Clever Repartee of Epictetus
intro: Epictetus advises that if a person speaks ill of you, make no defense, but answer: “He surely knew not of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these only.”

days.title: Zekle’s Courtin’
intro: Huldy, the rustic belle, sat alone peeling apples. She was bashful in her consciousness that Zekle would come soon. When he did, she merely blushed and timidly said: “Ma’s sprinklin’ clo’es,” and then—

days.title: Too Close to See the Battle
intro: England and France came to battle near Blenheim. Years later the people of Blenheim called it a “famous victory,” but could not tell whose victory it was.

readings.author: Robert Southey
readings.work: Southey’s After Blenheim and other poems
readings.title: After Blenheim and other poems

days.printed: Read: Southey’s After Blenheim and other poems

days.title: A College Boy Goes to Sea
intro: Leaving Harvard on account of ill health, Dana sought adventure and thrilling experience aboard a sailing vessel that rounded Cape Horn. He turned the dangers, hardships, and keen joys of a sailor’s life into a fascinating story.

readings.author: Richard Henry Dana, Jr.
readings.work: Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
readings.title: Two Years Before the Mast

days.printed: Read from Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
notes: Dana begins famous two-year voyage, Aug. 14, 1834.

days.title: Into Death’s Face He Flung This Song
intro: Charlemagne’s rear guard was attacked by the Basques in the valley of Roncesvaux. Roland, its leader, fought a courageous fight, and, though conquered, became immortal.
days.printed: Read from The Song of Roland

days.title: Inspiring Ritual of Temple Worship
intro: David—the psalm singer—knew the wondrous ways of the Lord and praised Him in his psalms. Burdened souls in all ages have found comfort in these songs that once were used in the gorgeous ritual of Jerusalem’s temple.

days.title: Three Walls Luther Saw
intro: Luther declared that the unreformed church had drawn its doctrines like three walls so closely about the people that they served not as protection but were the cause of untold misery and distress. This he hoped to relieve by the Reformation.
days.printed: Read: Luther’s Address to the Nobility

days.title: “I Took Her by the Hair and Dragged Her Up and Down”
intro: In Cellini’s day the model’s life was a hazardous one. Cellini’s Autobiography reveals how some models were treated. You will find it more thrilling than the most modern novel.

days.title: Roses Boiled in Wine
intro: Astonishing treatments and cures are related by Ambroise Paré, famed surgeon of the fifteenth century. One remedy, for instance, used to cure a distinguished nobleman, was red roses boiled in white wine,—and it was effective.
days.printed: Read from Paré’s Journeys in Diverse Places

days.title: Plot Against Eve
intro: Driven from Heaven, Satan meditated revenge. He decided his greatest opportunity to injure God was to bring sin to mankind. Satan’s plot against Eve is told by Milton.

days.title: Hidden Treasures in an Old Book
intro: A certain man was willed a Bible. He scorned the legacy until one day, penniless and downcast, he turned to the book for consolation. Imagine his amazement on finding hundred dollar bills between the pages. St. Augustine explains how he found even greater treasures in the Bible.
days.printed: Read from Confessions of St. Augustine

days.title: Aboard the Old Sailing Ships
intro: In the days when sailing ships plied the seven seas, common sailors were often subject to a brutal captain whose whim was law. Dana, a Boston college boy, makes an exciting story of his sea experiences.

readings.author: Richard Henry Dana, Jr.
readings.work: Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
readings.title: Two Years Before the Mast

days.printed: Read from Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast

days.title: Which Is a Beautiful Woman?
intro: The Hottentot thinks his wife beautiful. Every American believes his wife also to be beautiful. But the American and the Hottentot are quite different. What, after all, is Beauty?

readings.author: Edmund Burke
readings.work: Burke’s On the Sublime and Beautiful
readings.title: On the Sublime and Beautiful

days.printed: Read from Burke’s On the Sublime and Beautiful

days.title: Survivor’s Story of Vesuvius
intro: The eruption of Vesuvius that demolished Pompeii and buried thousands of people was witnessed by Pliny. He describes his panic-stricken flight with his mother from the doomed villa through falling ashes and sulphurous fumes. His famous uncle, the elder Pliny, lost his life while investigating the eruption and aiding refugees.
notes: Pliny witnessed eruption of Vesuvius, Aug. 24, 79 A. D.

days.title: Britain Saved by a Full Moon
intro: We to-day know that there is a direct relation between the moon and tides. When Julius Cæsar went to conquer Britain his transports were wrecked because he did not know the tides on the English coast; a knowledge of which might have changed the whole course of history.

days.title: The Prince of Wales Wins His Spurs
intro: A brilliant victory for the English king was gained in this battle, a fight in which vast numbers of French nobility, many princes, and the aged King John of Bohemia were slain. Froissart describes all in detail.

days.title: Priceless Treasures of Memory
intro: “A man’s a man for a’ that.” “Should auld acquaintance be forgot.” “To see her is to love her and love but her forever.” “Flow gently, sweet Afton.” Every stanza of Burns is treasured. How many have you stored up?
days.printed: Read from Burns’ Poems and Songs

days.title: The World’s Love Tragedy
intro: “Almighty God, I am undone.” With this cry of despair, Margaret witnessed the fiendish work of Faust, her lover, who bartered his immortal soul for worldly pleasure. A thrilling drama, based on a famous medieval legend.

days.title: Cleopatra Bewitches Mark Antony
intro: Cleopatra rode to meet Antony in a gilded barge with sails of purple; oars of silver beat time to the music of flutes and fifes and harps. She went as Venus, and her attendants were dressed as Cupids and Nymphs.
notes: Cleopatra dies after Antony’s suicide, Aug. 29, 30 B. C.

days.title: Simple Life in a Palace
intro: Every luxury, all the wealth in the world at his command—yet Marcus Aurelius, Emperor of haughty Rome, led a simple life even in a palace. He left his secret in his “Meditations.”

days.title: America’s Greatest Thinker
intro: Emerson was included in Dr. Eliot’s recent selection of the world’s ten greatest educators of all time. Here the great thinker discusses this force within man that makes him a scholar.

days.title: Expelled from College, Founded a City
intro: While at Oxford, Penn rejected the student’s gown and thereby created a furore. Later he founded a city where he sought to put his new ideas into practice.
days.printed: Read from Penn’s Some Fruits of Solitude
notes: Penn arrested for preaching in London, Sept. 1, 1670.

days.title: Too Great a Price for Love
intro: While his soldiers fought the battle of Actium, Antony fled to the arms of Cleopatra. By his flight he forfeited his right to an empire. Dryden’s story of Antony’s love makes us realize the folly of his infatuation for the Nile siren.
days.printed: Read from Dryden’s All for Love
notes: Battle of Actium, Sept. 2, 31 B. C.

days.title: Seven Years to Reach England
intro: Until 1783 the British refused to believe that the Liberty Bell had rung. Then they signed a treaty formally recognizing the Colonies as free and independent states.
notes: Treaty between England and the United States signed Sept. 3, 1783.

days.title: Voltaire Criticizes
intro: Voltaire’s daring courage led him to publish a series of letters which contained unfavorable comparisons of French customs with the English. For this he was threatened with the Bastille.
days.printed: Read: Voltaire’s Letters on the English

days.title: Survival of the Fittest
intro: Just as the individual has a definite length of life, so have species a limited duration. The progress and transition of the world, Darwin declares, will see the extinction of certain variants of human life.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Origin of Species
notes: Darwin first outlines his theory of natural selection, Sept. 5, 1857.

days.title: The Pride of All Scotchmen
intro: Many sons of Scotland have striven eagerly for the great place held by Sir Walter Scott. Carlyle describes the qualities that combined to make him the idol of his people and the master of historical romance.

days.title: The King’s Love
intro: There she was undoing her hair—the loveliest woman the eyes of men ever beheld, the light of wooing in her regal eyes. A longing for her overwhelmed the warrior-king.
days.printed: Read from Destruction of Da Derga’s Hostel

days.title: When Europe Lay Under Ice
intro: There was a time when the snow fell and did not melt in summer. Then from the frozen north there descended huge masses of ice that covered northern Europe and most of North America. Glaciers reveal a new world to us.
days.printed: Read from Helmholtz’s Ice and Glaciers

days.title: When Nature Beckons
intro: “There are days during the year,” says Emerson, “when the world of nature reaches perfection.” Can anyone escape this call, especially in the glorious Indian Summer?
notes: Emerson retires from the ministry, Sept. 9, 1832.

days.title: Famous Poet-Physician
intro: One of America’s famous New Englanders, Oliver Wendell Holmes, devoted his life principally to medicine. His name, however, was made famous through his poem, “Old Ironsides,” by which he saved America’s most famous battleship from destruction when her fighting days were ended.

days.title: Wages—Why and How Much?
intro: What regulates wages, on what do they depend? Adam Smith, world’s authority on economic problems, advances his theories on these matters.
days.printed: Read from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations

days.title: Love Letters of Elizabeth Browning
intro: In all literary history there is no happier love story than that of Elizabeth Barrett and Robert Browning. During their secret courtship Miss Barrett sent Browning many beautiful love letters written in verse.

days.title: Good That Came from a Game Pit
intro: From cockfighting, bear baiting, and like sports, the wife of John Bunyan converted him to a life of humility and reverence. While imprisoned for preaching, he used his idle time in writing a fantastic story of a soul’s salvation—probably the most famous allegory ever written.
notes: John Bunyan liberated and pardoned, Sept. 13, 1672.

days.title: Dante and St. Peter
intro: Dante, having journeyed through Hell and Purgatory, comes at last to St. Peter on his throne. St. Peter calls for the aid of St. James and St. John before passing final judgment on Dante’s righteousness.

days.title: Refused to Serve Three Terms
intro: George Washington retired to private life in 1796, entrusting “the preservation of the Union” to the “love of liberty.” His last appeal is a vital message to American citizens, as pertinent today as when he penned it.

days.title: Penalty for Silence
intro: “Such felons as stand mute [do not confess] are pressed to death by huge weights laid upon a board that lieth over their breast and a sharp stone under their backs.” Old English punishments, recorded by Holinshed, make startling reading.

days.title: Romance on a New England Farm
intro: “For of all sad words of tongue or pen, the saddest are these: ‘It might have been.’” On this theme Whittier based the story of a fair farmer girl and a rich judge.

days.title: Home After Storms and Adventures
