intro: “Every sight was full of beauty. We were coming back to our homes, and the signs of civilization from which we had been so long banished—” wrote Dana, as his ship entered Boston Harbor.

readings.author: Richard Henry Dana, Jr.
readings.work: Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
readings.title: Two Years Before the Mast

days.printed: Read from Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast
notes: Dana returns from two-year voyage, Sept. 18, 1836.

days.title: Humor That Survived Slavery
intro: Held as a Moorish slave for five years, Cervantes was submitted to almost daily tortures. But even the horrors of slavery could not dull his sense of humor, as evinced by his most witty and amusing novel.

days.title: Women’s Rights in the Harem
intro: The Koran defines the powers of a husband over his wives. Thus a woman unfaithful to her lord may be walled up alive.
notes: Mohammed arrives at Kuba after “The Flight,” Sept. 20, 622.

days.title: Æneas and the Old Witch
intro: The Sybil, an old witch, personally conducts Æneas through the gate and into the jaws of hell, where terrors abound on every hand and frightful mysterious forms rule. There he is told of the greatness and glory that was to come.

days.title: A King for a Souvenir
intro: In the days when kings rode to battle leading their troops it was possible to make good the boast of the doughboy: “I’ll bring you a king for a souvenir.”
notes: Froissart dates Battle of Poitiers, Sept. 22, 1356.

days.title: Dying Concerns Every Man
intro: The Romans made an art of dying. The Egyptians looked on death with complacency. Moderns fear it. Montaigne argues that the purpose of philosophy is to teach men how to die.

readings.author: Michel de Montaigne
readings.work: Montaigne’s To Learn How to Die
readings.title: To Learn How to Die

days.printed: Read from Montaigne’s To Learn How to Die

days.title: Citizens Lured from Their Homes
intro: When the serpent of Minerva disappeared from her temple, the priests said that the goddess had left Athens for the sea. Moreover, the oracles urged the Athenians to seek safety in their ships. Themistocles prompted these deceits. Why?

days.title: A Courtship of Twenty Years
intro: John Stuart Mill in his autobiography boldly tells of his love for his friend’s wife. After twenty years, she was freed from her first husband and was happily married to John Stuart Mill. Read the account of Mill’s courtship.

days.title: And the World Rocked with Laughter
intro: The gaunt lunatic, Don Quixote, saw the world through glasses colored with romanticism that had gone out of style hundreds of years before he was born. Cervantes made the world laugh at the exaggerated stories it had been devouring.
notes: Printing of Cervantes’ “Don Quixote” licensed, Sept. 26, 1604.

days.title: Pascal’s Fundamentals of Religion
intro: To-day we have Fundamentalists and Modernists, each striving for the same goal. Pascal, two hundred and fifty years ago, gave his precepts of the fundamentals of religious thought.

days.title: He Introduced the Germ
intro: Proof that germs cause many contagious diseases was established by Louis Pasteur. His discoveries revolutionized modern science and lessened the ravages of every type of disease.

days.title: Prophet of 400 Million People
intro: Confucius was a Chinese magistrate in 500 B. C. He lost the favor of the Emperor and wandered from city to city, teaching and giving counsel. After his death, Emperor and people alike bowed before his shrine.

days.title: A Gentleman According to Emerson
intro: An etiquette book and a good tailor do not always produce a gentleman—neither does the Social Register include only gentlemen. Emerson by quaint stories tells how fashion and manners combine to make that rare product—a gentleman.

days.title: Princes To-day and Yesterday
intro: To-day the chief duty of a prince is to be the nation’s friend maker. Years ago princes desired supreme power and, by fair means or foul, strove for control. Machiavelli was a guide for such ambitious princes.
notes: Machiavelli’s model prince sent to France as papal legate, Oct. 1, 1498.

days.title: Veteran Tells of Indian War
intro: Just before Darwin visited Bahia Blanca, an Indian insurrection had been ruthlessly put down. A veteran of the Indian war told Darwin how Indians had been treated.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle
notes: Darwin returns from South America, Oct. 2, 1836.

days.title: Good Enough for Chaucer
intro: When polite English society conversed in French—considering English a vulgar tongue, fit only for servants and working people—Chaucer, nevertheless, wrote poems in this “vulgar” English, which charm us because of their quaint words.

days.title: His Mouth Full of Pebbles
intro: The man who put pebbles in his mouth and orated to the sea, shaved one-half of his head so that he would be obliged to stay at home until he had perfected his oratory—a strange method of attaining eminence, but a successful one.

days.title: Amateur Athlete in Old Athens
intro: A boxer in public games desired to study philosophy at Athens. There were no furnaces to tend, no tables to wait on, no books or magazines to peddle, yet this sturdy young Greek managed to work his way through college.
days.printed: Read from Newman’s University Life at Athens

days.title: The Atrocious Spectacle of October 6th
intro: Wakened by the death cries of her sentry, Marie Antoinette, Queen of France, fled by a secret passage from the fury of a vile mob. The royal family was arrested and taken to Paris to await their fate.
days.printed: Read from Burke’s Revolution in France

days.title: An Uncanonized American Saint
intro: John Woolman was the foremost leader of the early Quakers and contributed much to the spiritual life of the American Colonies. He was a pioneer in the crusade against slavery.
days.printed: Read from The Journal of John Woolman

days.title: Fielding’s Parody Becomes History
intro: Fielding wrote a lengthy story to burlesque a novel of Richardson. But the travesty overshot its mark. Instead of a mere parody, it became a masterpiece.
days.printed: Read: Fielding’s Preface to Joseph Andrews

days.title: Songs Shake the Walls of Jericho
intro: Do you know that many of your favorite hymns have echoed for hundreds of years through vast cathedrals, and resounded from the walls of Jericho during the Crusades?
notes: Newman, author of “Lead, Kindly Light,” baptized Oct. 9, 1845.

days.title: A Fugitive in Boy’s Clothes
intro: The romance-stricken Don Quixote sees a fair youth seated by the side of a stream, “his feet like two crystals, his hands like snowflakes.” The youth was a charming girl!
notes: Cervantes aided in the capture of Tunis, Oct. 10, 1573.

days.title: Æneas Flees from an Inconsolable Love
intro: Æneas, mythological founder of the Roman race, leaving Carthage and its lovely Queen Dido, was driven by a storm to the coast of Sicily. There the hospitality of King Acestes helped him to forget his relinquished love.

days.title: Columbus’ Letter Miraculously Found
intro: Historical documents, now priceless, were often used as wrapping paper. Rescued by chance was a letter of Columbus telling of his voyages—of the amazing bargains made with timid natives—of Amazon women who fought like men and made marriage treaties with cannibals.

days.title: Pagan Virtue Perpetuated
intro: A man of virtue, although a pagan, Marcus Aurelius ruled with benevolence and wisdom. Cruel in persecution of Christians as lawbreakers, no trace of this sternness appears in his writings.

days.title: No Spice and Little Gold
intro: All colonies are founded to gain territory or treasure. Spain expected spice and gold from Columbus’s expedition, but got no spice and little gold. Adam Smith tells the true motive of the colonizing Greeks, Romans, English, and Spaniards.
days.printed: Read from Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations

days.title: First Families of America
intro: “They are a people smooth and clean of body because of continually washing themselves—they eat all their enemies whom they kill or capture.” Amerigo Vespucci thus writes of the New World inhabitants.

readings.author: Amerigo Vespucci
readings.work: Vespucci’s Account of His First Voyage
readings.title: Account of His First Voyage

days.printed: Read: Vespucci’s Account of His First Voyage
notes: Amerigo Vespucci returns from first American voyage, Oct. 15, 1498.

days.title: When Medicine Was a Mystery
intro: Once physicians treated the sick with a mixture of medicine and charms. In those days medicine was regarded as a dark art like magic, and those practicing it formed guilds to protect themselves.

days.title: Reason His Only Religion
intro: The religion of Thomas Browne—a liberal man in a most intolerant time—was not taken from either Rome or Geneva, but from his own reason.
notes: Browne visited by Evelyn of “Evelyn Diary,” Oct. 17, 1671.

days.title: “If Winter Comes”
intro: From the title of a recently popular novel, we know that one prominent fiction writer of to-day was inspired by the verses of Shelley. Many others have also felt the stirring vigor of his poetry. What is your reaction?

days.title: Virtue in Smiles
intro: Weep if you must. It is far better than to repress your tears. But Leigh Hunt finds greater virtue in cheerfulness. Fanciful and graceful—his writings exerted a wholesome influence on all nineteenth century journalism.
notes: James Henry Leigh Hunt born Oct. 19, 1784.

days.title: Odysseus Adrift on a Raft
intro: The gods met in council and decreed that Odysseus be set adrift. Poseidon, God of the Sea, shattered the raft and Odysseus was cast ashore to encounter further adventures.

days.title: No Fault to Find with Old Age
intro: Cicero agrees with Browning that old age is the golden time of life, when the fruits of a well-spent life are harvested. Cicero, the wise Roman, welcomed old age for its gifts: wisdom, sound judgment, and contentment.
days.printed: Read from Cicero’s On Old Age

days.title: Swift’s Love Problems
intro: Swift was embarrassed by two women; Stella, whom he really loved, and Vanessa, with whom he had flirted and who had taken him seriously. Marriage to either one would break the heart of the other.

days.title: When Cæsar Turned the Tables
intro: When only a boy, Cæsar was captured by pirates. While awaiting ransom he entered into every sport and game with them. Once freed, he quickly returned with forces that captured the outlaws. Then he took deliberate revenge.

days.title: Clytemnestra Meets Her Rival
intro: Cassandra knew through a prophetic vision that a sword would pierce her heart. Agamemnon, her captor, took her to his home where an avenging wife, Clytemnestra, awaited. The tragedies of the doom that requited the sins of the House of Atreus are among the most powerful ever written.

days.title: It Greatly Encouraged Intrigue
intro: After the publication of Machiavelli’s “The Prince,” the Sultans became more addicted to strangling their brothers, tyrants became more merciless, and murderous plots increased. The influence of that book, as Macaulay points out, spread over Europe and Asia.
notes: Thomas Babington Lord Macaulay born Oct. 25, 1800.

days.title: Franklin Learned the Secret
intro: Poor at twenty, rich at forty, internationally famous at fifty. Benjamin Franklin once walked the streets of Philadelphia alone, poor, and with no education. Yet he rose to be a leader because he learned the secret of careful reading.
notes: Franklin made U. S. plenipotentiary in France, Aug. 26, 1778.

days.title: Fruit of Seven Years’ Silence
intro: Siddhartha Gautama, who became the god Buddha, renounced the world and spent seven years in meditation. Then one day, while sitting under a fig tree, he became inspired with exalted and sublime conceptions of life and death. The rest of his life was spent in teaching and converting mankind.

days.title: How Dice Taught Spelling
intro: Locke taught children by means of games. He tells of a game whereby children were taught to spell with dice on which the letters of the alphabet were pasted. This was more than 200 years before modern kindergarten methods. Today’s children would respond to such wise direction as Locke recommends.

days.title: Genius Rises from a Stable
intro: Though the son of a stable man, John Keats wrote the most exquisite and sublime poetry in our language. He was the friend of Shelley, Lord Byron, and the other literary leaders of the time—his genius recognized by all.

days.title: Geology’s Greatest Benefactor
intro: Lyell has been called the founder of modern geology. Darwin, the master scientist, called him “Geology’s Greatest Benefactor.” Lyell’s research revolutionized ideas on that subject.
days.printed: Read from Lyell’s The Progress of Geology

days.title: Witches Walk To-night
intro: Beware of magic! Once a year uneasy spirits are released and walk the earth from midnight until dawn. Spooks and goblins invade the most secure homes and the canniest must watch out for danger lurking in every dark corner.

days.title: Last Strokes of Shakespeare’s Pen
intro: Monsters of the earth, weird creatures of the air, magic romance, and shipwreck are mingled by a master hand in his thrilling drama. The fanciful, enchanting “Tempest” is the last work of the great bard of Stratford.
notes: “The Tempest” performed at Queen Elizabeth’s court, Nov. 1, 1611.

days.title: Journey Through a Hot Country
intro: Dante recorded the awful scenes of a journey through the pits of the underworld, and wrote in such a vivid, realistic way that men tremble at the terrors depicted.

days.title: Letters to an Emperor
intro: Pliny sought the advice of the Emperor Trajan for dealing with the Christians who were alarmingly on the increase. He casually relates how he had tortured two Christians.

days.title: Gold or Glory?
intro: Polyeucte, an Armenian noble, wanted to become a Christian. If he were baptized, he would have to give up his high position, his wealth and his pagan wife. Was the heavenly crown worth this sacrifice?

days.title: Costly Opinion on Divorce
intro: A divorce always means trouble for some one. So with Sir Thomas More when he refused to agree with King Henry over the king’s separation. More was made to pay one of the highest prices ever paid for a difference of opinion.

readings.author: William Roper
readings.work: Roper’s Life of Sir Thomas More
readings.title: Life of Sir Thomas More

days.printed: Read from Roper’s Life of Sir Thomas More

days.title: A Genius Needs Few Tools
intro: Two sticks, a table, and a pail were the commonplace implements used by Michael Faraday to demonstrate great scientific truths.
notes: Faraday sends “Experimental Researches” to Royal Society, Nov. 6, 1845.

days.title: The Voice from a Stone-Dead City
intro: Suddenly all the sinful city’s inhabitants were turned to stone. When a beautiful woman from Bagdad came to the dead city, night overtook her there. Sleeping in the palace, she was awakened by a man’s voice calling.
days.printed: Read from The Thousand and One Nights

days.title: Blind But Unconquered
intro: Milton’s indomitable courage kept him at his work even after he lost his sight. Blind, he dictated a sequel to his “Paradise Lost,” which he called “Paradise Regained.”

days.title: Once War Songs, Now Pious Prayers
intro: The Psalms have been an inspiration to men in many ages. They have become so associated with the peaceful spirit of Christianity that we forget some of them were once war songs and songs of triumph.

days.title: A Poet Who Piped for His Supper
intro: Goldsmith traveled through Belgium, France, and Italy, winning his daily bread by playing at farmhouses. He wrote the most brilliant comedy, the best novel, and the finest poem of his age.

days.title: America’s Doughboy Glorified
intro: The youth of America—typified in the doughboy of the past war—was gloriously portrayed by Walt Whitman. He also sang of the vast plains and the beauty of America.

days.title: Story of the First Dresses
intro: Milton’s version tells how the Serpent induced Eve to eat the forbidden fruit. Eve offered it to Adam. Then they became conscious for the first time that they were not clothed.
notes: John Milton married second wife, Nov. 12, 1656.

days.title: When Carthage Was Monte Carlo
intro: Carthage was the playground of the ancient world. In that city of many sins, Augustine was a leader of the revels. His conversion to Christianity amazed those who knew him.
days.printed: Read from the Confessions of St. Augustine

days.title: He Worried About It
intro: We wonder if the man who worried about the “scientifical” prediction that “The sun’s heat will give out in ten million years more,” had read Lyell on the gradual changes in the earth’s surface.

days.title: Food Profiteers 300 Years Ago
intro: Food profiteering was as active in plague-stricken Milan 300 years ago as in modern times. Shops were stormed for food. Read how the Council strove heroically to fix fair rates.
days.printed: Read from Manzoni’s I Promessi Sposi
notes: Sale of corn and flour regulated in Milan, Nov. 15, 1629.

days.title: Just Before the Gold Rush
intro: When the glorious Western coast was only partly settled, Dana visited the Presidios. He saw frontier life at a time when Spanish splendor still gilded California.
days.printed: Read from Two Years Before the Mast

days.title: At Thirty Scott Began to Write
intro: Are you curious about famous people, their lives, habits, personalities? Carlyle discusses the intimate life of his illustrious countryman, and reveals Scott, the man, and Scott, the genius who entertained Christendom with his stories.

days.title: Apple or Son the Arrow’s Mark
intro: The arrow shot from his bow with a twang and whizzed through the air. Tell covered his eyes, fearing to see where the arrow hit. Then the shout of triumph, a shout of the people and not of the tyrant—but the end was not yet.
notes: William Tell incident, legendary date, Nov. 18, 1307.

days.title: No Man Knows His Resting Place
intro: A barge with black sails bearing three black robed queens with crowns of gold carried away the dying King Arthur. Will they bring him back and fulfill Merlin’s prophecy?
notes: Queen Victoria appointed Tennyson poet laureate, Nov. 19, 1850.

days.title: Old Stories Ever New
intro: When the cold winds howled about the thatched huts of the German peasant, the mother drew her children to her side and told them stories. Collected and retold by the Grimm brothers, these stories have perennial charm.

days.title: Bargains in Wives
intro: The beautiful daughters of the Circassians were in demand for the seraglios of the Turkish Sultan. Voltaire tells how these beauties were protected from smallpox centuries before modern vaccination.

days.title: How a Queen Died for Love
intro: Deserted by her lover, Queen Dido applied to her heart the only balm that could ease her pain.

days.title: Less Than Star Dust
intro: According to Pascal, a man is not even as significant as a speck of star dust in the universe. Pascal’s thoughts on the subject are startling to the modern reader, and they furnish rich food for the imagination.

days.title: The Book that Upset Tennessee
intro: The signal for the beginning of a great controversy, still raging, was the publication of Darwin’s “Origin of Species.” This was the first complete statement of the evolution theory, which had been privately advanced but never publicly taught. A new epoch in science dates from this great work.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Origin of Species

days.title: Cupid as a Shoemaker
intro: We are indebted to Thomas Dekker for one of the most humorous characters in all Elizabethan literature; namely, Simon Eyre, an old shoemaker whose affairs became hilariously involved with those of the gentry.
days.printed: Read from Dekker’s The Shoemaker’s Holiday

days.title: Shakespeare Should Be Heard
intro: Charles Lamb, favorite essayist, thought that no stage could do justice to Shakespeare’s tragedies. He advocated reading the plays, and with the imagination costuming the players and building the gorgeous scenery in a way equaled by no scene painter or costumer.

readings.author: Charles Lamb
readings.work: Lamb On the Tragedies of Shakspere
readings.title: On the Tragedies of Shakspere

days.printed: Read: Lamb On the Tragedies of Shakspere

days.title: What Land is This?
intro: In wondrous Utopia pearls and precious stones were used as playthings for little children. Gold rings and bracelets were only worn by outcasts, while great golden chains shackled criminals and felons. When ambassadors from foreign lands came in fine raiment, the Utopians treated the plainest dressed as the greatest: the others seemed to them like children.
days.printed: Read from Sir Thomas More’s Utopia

days.title: Poems Made from Visions
intro: “To see a world in a grain of sand, and a heaven in a wild flower—” Such was the exaltation of the mysticism of William Blake, who reflected in his poetry the ecstasy of his visions. Simplicity is the keynote of his genius.

days.title: How Ideas Originate
intro: Did you ever stop to think just how you thought? What inner emotions, what outer influences make up the fathomless depths of mind and intellect? Hume explains how we draw our thoughts, then clumsily put them into tangible shape called ideas.

readings.author: David Hume
readings.work: Hume’s Of the Origin of Ideas
readings.title: Of the Origin of Ideas

days.printed: Read: Hume’s Of the Origin of Ideas

days.title: “Don’ts” for Conversation
intro: To harp on one’s illnesses, giving all the symptoms and circumstances, has been a blemish on conversation for ages. Two hundred years ago Swift complained of persons who continually talked about themselves.

days.title: Are Skeptics Faulty Thinkers?
intro: Offhand we say a skeptic is one who doubts everything. But does he? And are his doubts caused by too much learning, or too little? Berkeley presents both sides of skepticism.

days.title: Practical Jokes in King Arthur’s Day
intro: Attacked in fun by two masked knights, Sir Galahad smote one so that both horse and rider went down. Turning on the other jester, he slashed open his helmet.

days.title: Met the Gods of Ten Thousand Worlds
intro: After three awesome messengers have issued three warnings, the gods of ten thousand worlds decide who is to be the new Buddha. Then the parents, the conception, the birth of the god-child demand constant vigilance.
days.printed: Read: The Birth of the Buddha

days.title: The Queen Weds a Poor Stranger
intro: Æneas and Dido, world-famous lovers, while hunting in the forest, were trapped in a cave by a furious storm. There the marriage between the proud African queen and the homeless wanderer was completed.

days.title: Poems by an Artist’s Model
intro: So beautiful that many painters sought her for a model—Christina Rossetti, sister of the famous poet, Dante Rossetti, combined with her unusual beauty a rare poetic sense.

days.title: Moralizing as a Seductive Art
intro: “The Vision of Mirza” and “Westminster Abbey,” first printed in “The Spectator,” are examples of Addison’s wondrous gift of expression. He leads us to higher realms.
notes: Last issue of “The Spectator” published Dec. 6, 1712.

days.title: What Cicero Least Expected
intro: After being governor of Sicily, Cicero returned to Rome expecting a hero’s welcome. When he asked what the Romans thought of his recent achievements, he received an astounding answer.
notes: Cicero slain by Mark Antony’s soldiers, Dec. 7, 43 B. C.

days.title: Dream Women Shaped His Destiny
intro: De Quincy imagined that three women were sent to him so that he might know the depths of his soul. Real women could not have wielded greater influence. It is fortunate that everyone does not meet these weird women.

readings.author: Thomas De Quincey
readings.work: Levana and Our Ladies of Sorrow

days.printed: Read: Levana and Our Ladies of Sorrow

days.title: Slavery’s Last Stand
intro: By the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 stringent laws were made to prevent assistance being given to any slaves attempting to escape. The antislavery answer to these laws was a perfection of the “Underground Railroad.”

days.title: Benvenuto Boasts of Gallantry
intro: Taking offense at a soldier who made advances toward his favorite lady, Cellini jumped from the window, knife in hand, to avenge himself. This incident was recorded with characteristic conceit by Cellini in his amazing diary.

days.title: The Most Dashing Figure in Athens
intro: The handsome Alcibiades, cunning in politics, bold in war, was the lion of Athenian society until he violated the secrets of a mysterious religious cult. Then all outraged Athens united to dash their idol to the ground.

days.title: How the Glorious News was Carried to Aix
intro: Three brave men began the heroic ride from Ghent to Aix. Only one man arrived to tell the thrilling story of the tempestuous ride. In one of his most bewitching poems, in lines that haunt the memory, Browning retells the story.

days.title: To the South Seas with the Gallant Drake
intro: A famous voyage was Sir Francis Drake’s around the world. Drake’s crew, the first white men to visit many parts of the world, received amazing receptions from the natives.
days.printed: Read from Drake’s Voyage Round the World
notes: Sir Francis Drake embarked for South Seas, Dec. 13, 1577.

days.title: Pastoral Poems and Politics
intro: The many-sided Marvell, who wielded a pen that was both feared and courted, is seen at his best in stirring verse. “A Garden,” “Prospect of Flowers,” with the “Horatian Ode upon Cromwell,” show the power of his genius.

days.title: Odysseus Talks with Ghosts
intro: This is another of those marvelous and unforgetable tales of the wandering Odysseus. The fantasy takes him into regions where he discourses with deceased heroes.

days.title: How Man’s Courtship Differs from Animal’s
intro: Beauty is an important factor in the attraction between man and woman. It is knowing beauty that differentiates man from the animals, which only require that their mates be of the same species.
days.printed: Read from Burke’s The Sublime and Beautiful

days.title: Dies on the Eve of Her Son’s Conversion
intro: The mother of St. Augustine prayed unceasingly for her son’s conversion. The most touching, most soul-revealing writing St. Augustine did is in the description of his mother’s death.
days.printed: Read from Confessions of St. Augustine

days.title: For a Gentleman
intro: Every schoolboy asks: “What’s the use of learning Latin?” John Locke, one of the greatest educators of all time, maintains that Latin is absolutely essential to a well-bred gentleman, and explains why.
days.printed: Read from Some Thoughts Concerning Education

days.title: Samson Finds a Champion
intro: The mighty Samson was blinded while a captive of the Philistines. He sought revenge—a revenge devastating and costly. Milton, himself a giant of intellect, blind and imprisoned, wrote of this sightless giant of other days.

days.title: Egypt Visited by the First Reporter
intro: All phases of life were pictured by Herodotus in his history. Like a modern newspaper reporter, he combines weird stories, scandals, and battle accounts with descriptions of places, persons, and sights about town.
days.printed: Read from Herodotus’ An Account of Egypt

days.title: “Madam Bubble” Not to Be Discouraged
intro: “Madam Bubble,” or this vain world, presented both herself and her purse to the wayfarer. Repulsed and scorned, yet she serenely flaunts her bribes enticingly before his bewildered eyes.
notes: John Bunyan made leader of Non-Conformist congregation, Dec. 21, 1671.

days.title: Rubbing Noses in New Zealand
intro: Darwin, in exploring New Zealand, finds cannibalism, tattooing, and many weird customs among the natives. Instead of shaking hands, the salutation is by rubbing noses.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle
notes: Darwin visits New Zealand natives, Dec. 22, 1835.

days.title: Saved from a Bonfire of Books
intro: If all the books in the world were on fire, some men would risk their lives to save certain priceless writings: the world’s classics. Sainte-Beuve here tells why.
days.printed: Read: Sainte-Beuve’s What Is a Classic?

days.title: Christmas Made a Dull Day
intro: Before the Reformation in England almost every third day was a holy day. But the Puritans abolished all the holy days, even Christmas.

days.title: The Christmas Story
intro: Luke was a Greek physician, a man of culture, trained in the best universities of the ancient world. He became imbued with the spirit of Christ, and wrote the most beautiful story of the birth and life of Jesus.
days.printed: Read from the Gospel of St. Luke

days.title: Silence Cost Her a Kingdom
intro: Cordelia, daughter of old King Lear, could not convince her father of her love for him. Afterward, when misfortunes made him accept her aid, he learned too late of her real devotion.
notes: “King Lear” presented at Queen Elizabeth’s court, Dec. 26, 1606.

days.title: Million-Year-Old Islands
intro: It was the new-old lands that Darwin visited on his voyage of the “Beagle.” The strange specimens of prehistoric life he saw there made the world gape and shudder.
days.printed: Read from Darwin’s Voyage of the Beagle
notes: Charles Darwin begins voyage in the “Beagle,” Dec. 27, 1831.

days.title: Ho! for the Spanish Main!
intro: Drake with a fleet of twenty-five ships and twenty-three hundred men sets sail to plunder and lay waste Spain’s treasure hoards in the New World. Gold and silver bar, nuggets and jewels awaited the bold adventurers.

days.title: These Guests Outstayed Their Welcome
intro: After twenty years’ absence, Odysseus returned home to find his house filled with strangers rioting and wasting his treasure. Crafty Odysseus, with the aid of his son and the gods, devised a bold plan to rid his home of the unwelcome guests.

days.title: Dana Meets a Tattooed Sailor
intro: Dana’s description of the picturesque, pre-gold-rush California is unique. While he was on the Pacific coast he met a British sailor who was elaborately tattooed and of an unforgetable appearance and personality.

days.printed: Read from Dana’s Two Years Before the Mast

days.title: Curiosity and Interest as Guides to Reading
intro: The most unhappy man, Carlyle says, is the man who has no real work—no interest in life. To avoid this miserable state, he advises faithful and diligent reading along the lines dictated by curiosity and interest.
